item.title: Where the Tide Left Him
item.description: The Waking Shores smelled of ash and promise — the way new continents always do before the cartographers ruin everything with accurate maps. Burrly arrived at Wingrest Embassy with the particular impatience of a man who has sailed through storms and sees no reason a dragon-infested coastline should slow him down. He’s Kul Tiran. They’re built like that.
item.content:encoded:
The Waking Shores smelled of ash and promise — the way new continents always do before the cartographers ruin everything with accurate maps. Burrly arrived at Wingrest Embassy with the particular impatience of a man who has sailed through storms and sees no reason a dragon-infested coastline should slow him down. He’s Kul Tiran. They’re built like that.

The djaradin had awoken, which — the chronicler notes with some fatigue — is what ancient enemies always do the moment fresh adventurers wander into range. Burrly was handed a quest before his boots were dry: Excuse the Mess. The mess, as it turned out, was the djaradin. The excuse was his axe. He got to work.

What followed was the familiar rhythm of a man finding his footing in a strange land. He rescued dragon whelps from the Scalecracker Keep, reported for duty at the Obsidian Citadel, and learned — as all warriors eventually learn in the Dragon Isles — that everything here is on fire and at least half of it wants to kill you. The other half just wants you to fill out paperwork. He did both. Eight quests in thirty-five minutes is not the pace of a tourist. It is the pace of a man who knows the tide waits for no one, not even on a continent suspended in the sky.

Along the way his hands found the old trades: mining and herbalism. He cracked open heated ore deposits and pulled rousing fire from the earth, stuffing the spoils into whatever pockets remained. The chronicler has watched a thousand adventurers gather herbs and ore. None of them look proud doing it. Burrly didn’t either, but he looked competent, which is rarer.

He left the Dragon Isles at level fifteen, which is to say: still small enough that a dragon would need to squint to notice him, but no longer so small that a djaradin could ignore him. Progress of a sort. The ladder extends upward forever, but the first rungs are the only ones that feel anything like flying.

Then — somewhere between the Waking Shores and the Eastern Kingdoms, in the space between logging out and logging back in — Burrly changed. When he reappeared for his second session of the day, he was eighty. Not the slow climb of experience, but the sudden arrival of everything at once: Battle Stance and Defensive Stance, Mortal Strike and Overpower, Heroic Leap, Bladestorm, Colossus Smash — a dozen abilities flooding his muscle memory like a tide coming in. The chronicler has seen this before. The how matters less than the what-next.

The what-next took him to Hammerfall in the Arathi Highlands, where he accepted three writs of Notoriety — with the Vizier, the Weaver, the General — the kind of bureaucratic death warrant that passes for paperwork at level eighty. He abandoned a trading post report and a treasure hunt along the way, which says something about priorities when a man has fifty-two million gold coming and twenty-two minutes to spend it.

A stop in Stormwind. Cathedral Square. A quest called Midnight, accepted with the quiet gravity of a thing whose name sounds less like a task and more like a prophecy. Then the bank: fifty million gold, arriving in a single transaction the way mail from the auction house does when you’ve been away long enough for the market to miss you. He didn’t pause to count it. He bought the tabard of Kul Tiras — the anchor sigil worn across his chest like a second heart — and kept moving.

Stormwind gave way to Silvermoon, the spires of Quel’Thalas rising pink and gold against a sky that has never quite forgiven what happened here. He accepted Eversong. He completed Adventuring in Midnight. He explored the Bazaar, the Sanctum of Light. The city remembered him, or at least its factions did: the Silvermoon Court welcomed him as a friend, and Valeera Sanguinar herself — exalted, which in Blood Elf reckoning probably means she didn’t have him followed. Slayer’s Duellum remained neutral. Some things you earn. Some things you don’t.

Fifty-seven minutes total across two sessions. Three levels gained in the morning, a lifetime of abilities unlocked by afternoon, and enough gold to make a goblin weep into his ledger. Burrly ended the day where the tide left him: Silvermoon City, a tabard on his back and a quest called Eversong still glowing in his log, unanswered, like a question the sun hasn’t risen on yet.

item.title: The Voyage Out
item.description: The gold arrived before the quest did.
item.content:encoded:
The gold arrived before the quest did.

Burrly stood in the Harbormaster’s Office in Boralus — a Kul Tiran warrior with the kind of build that suggests he’s won more arguments with his fists than with his words — when his coin purse suddenly contained five million gold pieces. The chronicler, who has watched adventurers scrape together coppers for decades, set down his quill and stared at the ledger for a long moment. Enough gold to fund a small war. Enough gold to buy a fleet. Enough to make a goblin trade prince develop a nervous twitch.

Burrly did what any sensible man does when suddenly wealthy beyond reason: he went straight to Stormwind and spent nearly half of it before sundown.

The trip was official, at least. “For the Alliance” — the quest-giver said it with the weight of ceremony, and Burrly, who understands that paperwork is the true endgame of every hero’s journey, accepted without comment. He crossed the sea, presented himself at the Stormwind Embassy, and was handed a Tabard of Kul Tiras as if the anchor on his chest needed official recognition. He put it on immediately. A man doesn’t forget where he came from, even when his pockets say he never has to go back.

Then the spending began. Six bank tabs purchased in rapid, mechanical succession — the “Safer Deposit” achievement, as though anyone in Azeroth has ever felt safe about anything stored in a bank. Sunfire Silk Backpacks, four of them, bought like a man who expects to fill every one. An Arcanoweave Reagent Rucksack for good measure. Half a million gold on bank tabs alone. The goblin clerks, creatures not known for their emotional range, looked genuinely moved.

With the banking sorted — because even a warrior headed for the Dragon Isles needs somewhere to keep his rocks — Burrly turned to the practical arts. He learned to mine, cracking open the earth with the same enthusiasm he brings to cracking skulls. Smelt Copper: the first recipe every aspiring smith learns and immediately forgets exists once better ores present themselves. He learned to gather herbs. And he learned to fish, because whatever else a Kul Tiran becomes — warrior, wanderer, suddenly-wealthy eccentric — he is first and always a man of the sea.

The journey to the Dragon Isles proceeded with the grim efficiency of bureaucracy. “The Dragon Isles Await.” “Aspectral Invitation.” “Whispers on the Winds.” Quest after quest of people telling Burrly things he already knew, in rooms he’d already visited, about threats he’d already agreed to face. The chronicler has watched a thousand heroes run this same gauntlet. None of them have ever looked happy about it.

Then, at last, the ship. The Wild Coast materializing out of the ocean mist. The Waking Shores spreading before him — volcanic, primordial, a land that had been sleeping since before the Sundering and was still blinking awake. The chronicler will say this for the Dragon Isles: they know how to make an entrance.

Burrly learned to climb. The world — and here the chronicler means the strange metaphysics that govern this realm — taught him to detect anomalies and bypass mechanisms, skills his people traditionally addressed by hitting things until they stopped being problems. Progress, of a sort. He also learned to fish again, because the Dragon Isles are very particular about fishing credentials. Two different fishing instructors had to sign off. The sea, apparently, has standards now.

The first creatures fell to Mortal Strike. A Chitin Dreadbringer dropped from something with too many legs, and Burrly picked it up, tested its weight, and kept walking. Warriors who pause to admire their weapons rarely live to use them twice. He learned Berserker Rage at level twelve — which is exactly what it sounds like and exactly what you want a man of his size to bring to a fight.

Two level-ups in forty-two minutes. The chronicler notes this without judgment. Some days, the world simply yields.

He abandoned one quest. Something about lava beetles and artisan supplies. A man with nearly three million gold remaining in his pockets can afford to be selective. The beetles, one assumes, will find another supplier.

By the time Burrly reached the Wingrest Embassy, the sun had set and his quest log held more open threads than a goblin’s ledger: Wrathion was missing, elementals were encroaching, someone needed quality assurance, and a frankly inexplicable quest about a bar tab barrel had been completed — a task so absurd the chronicler suspects it was written while drunk and accepted under the same condition.

He logged out in the Waking Shores. Twelve levels. Three professions. A rare blade on his back. Gold enough to make a dragon consider early retirement. The chronicler poured another drink and watched the embers settle in the hearth. Some heroes claw their way to fortune inch by bloody inch, copper by grudging copper. Others arrive with it already in their pockets, as if the universe had placed a bet and was waiting to see if it paid off.

The Dragon Isles await. Wrathion is missing. The beetles, for now, are someone else’s problem.

item.title: Cron stormwind gates
item.description: Beta chapter. All progress resets on November 4th.
item.content:encoded:
Beta chapter. All progress resets on November 4th.

The Mine and the Marble City

The kobold’s candle guttered out just as Cron’s blade found its mark. In the dark of Fargodeep Mine, that small death bought a heartbeat of silence before the next pair of glowing eyes came shuffling around the corner. They always come shuffling.

Cron spent the better part of his morning down there, trading swings with the rat-faced miners who had apparently been hoarding gold dust — because someone in Goldshire, a town literally named after the stuff, decided they’d rather not dig it up themselves. He emerged with a sack of the promised powder, a few new scars, and that particular clarity of purpose that only comes from being underground long enough to forget what the sky looks like. The chronicler has seen this look before. It never lasts.

Back in Goldshire, the turn-ins came fast. Six quests resolved in half an hour — a pace that suggests either competence or desperation, and the chronicler has stopped trying to tell the difference. The kobold candles went to the quartermaster. The fishy peril — some business with murlocs near the lake, the sort of errand veterans accept without asking questions because the answers are always worse — resolved itself without ceremony. He even returned a book, which is more than most warriors manage in a career. One of the new camp-training quests, part of the strange bloom of tasks that has appeared across Elwynn in recent weeks. The chronicler notes the anomaly and pours another cup.

At the Lion’s Pride Inn, Marshal Dughan’s people taught Cron to wrap a wound and brew a minor healing potion. Useful skills. He’ll need both. The innkeeper watered the ale as she always does, and Cron paid for it anyway as they always do.

Then came the road to Stormwind.

Every human adventurer remembers their first approach to the city gates. The Valley of Heroes opens before you like a promise written in marble — statues of legends staring down with stone eyes that somehow manage to look disappointed. Cron crossed the threshold at level seven, which is either early or late depending on which grizzled veteran you ask at which hour of which tavern. The chronicler has asked them all. The answers remain contradictory.

Twenty-nine minutes of work. Eight hundred and ninety-two copper earned, one hundred spent — a profit margin that would make a goblin weep with envy. He logged out somewhere in the city proper, the towers of Stormwind at his back and the rest of Azeroth still entirely ahead of him.

The chronicler sets down the quill. The room at the inn is paid through morning. Outside, the Elwynn night is quiet, which means something is probably hunting.

Next: the city has quests. The city always has quests.

item.title: Lemmy first step
item.description: Beta chapter. All progress resets on November 4th.
item.content:encoded:
Beta chapter. All progress resets on November 4th.

A Shadow in Northshire

The chronicler had barely sharpened his quill when the boy was already gone.

Three minutes. That is how long Lemmy spent in the world today — just enough time for the abbey’s census-takers to record his name, for the factions of the Alliance to note his existence in their ledgers, and for one kobold to die badly in the vineyard. The chronicler has watched a thousand adventurers take their first steps into Northshire Valley. Few of them left again so quickly. Fewer still carried the particular weight this one does.

Because Lemmy is a warlock.

Now, Northshire Abbey trains paladins and priests — the kind of holy folk who regard fel magic the way a baker regards a rat in the flour. Yet here he was, accepting Brother Paxton’s blessing with one hand while the other, the chronicler suspects, was already tracing the faint outline of a summoning circle in his palm. The abbey’s records show him as “friendly” to Stormwind, Ironforge, Gnomeregan, and Darnassus alike. Paperwork has a way of smoothing over the uncomfortable details. The chronicler has learned to read between the lines.

His first task was “A Threat Within” — the standard Northshire opener. Kill the kobolds in the vineyard. Every human who has ever picked up a sword in this kingdom has killed those same kobolds. They respawn, or perhaps they simply never learn. Lemmy dispatched the required number, collected no reward but the forty points of experience the world doles out for such things, and immediately accepted the follow-up: “Kobold Camp Cleanup.”

And then — nothing. The connection severed. The boy vanished from the chronicler’s sight as abruptly as he had appeared, leaving behind an accepted quest, an unsheathed dagger, and the distinct impression of unfinished business.

The chronicler does not know whether Lemmy logged out because his mother called him to supper, or because the weight of what he is becoming settled onto his shoulders for the first time. Warlocks are not born in Northshire. They choose it. And choices made in the shadow of an abbey have a way of echoing.

He earned no copper. He spent none. He gained no level. But he accepted a quest that will take him deeper into the woods, closer to the things that whisper from the treeline after dark.

The chronicler will be watching when he returns. The quill is ready. The ink is wet.

The fire crackles. The mug is empty. The vineyard kobolds have already forgotten him.

Next: the camp cleanup awaits. The woods are patient.

item.title: Zixxy zephras isle
item.description: Beta chapter. All progress resets on November 4th.
item.content:encoded:
Beta chapter. All progress resets on November 4th.

The Skyborne and the Stranger

The chronicler does not often find himself on Zephras Isle. It is a place apart — a shard of land adrift in seas that do not appear on any map the cartographers of Stormwind would recognize. The High Order Skyborne call it home, and they do not encourage visitors. Which is, of course, precisely why adventurers keep washing up there.

Zixxy arrived at Thendal Village with frost still clinging to his robes. A mage of the Skyborne, level four and climbing, the kind of young spellcaster who has already learned that fire solves most problems and that the remaining problems require more fire. He spent eighteen minutes on the isle today. The chronicler spent most of them squinting through salt spray and trying to keep his ink from running.

The morning began with blood. “Aggressive Encroachment” — the Skyborne do not name their problems gently — sent Zixxy into Thendal Cave to clear out whatever had decided the village’s doorstep was now its territory. He emerged with cave dust in his hair, a notch of experience that pushed him to level five, and the quiet satisfaction of a man who has just proven that arcane missiles outperform teeth. The chronicler notes: thirty-five experience for discovering the cave itself, as though the world rewards you simply for stumbling into the right wrong place.

Then came the stranger.

Scorpio-Falcone arrived without preamble — the way companions often do in these borderland zones, where the usual protocols of introduction give way to the more practical business of not dying alone. They formed a party of two. The chronicler watched from the cliffside as they fell into rhythm: Zixxy’s frost slowing the enemy, Scorpio’s blade finishing the work. The Foul Matriarch — some bloated matriarch of whatever had infested the cave — fell to their combined effort. One hundred copper reward. Five hundred and fifty experience. The kind of payout that says the threat was real.

They both reached level five within moments of each other. The chronicler has seen friendships forged over less, and rivalries over more. Which this becomes remains unwritten.

Two new quests accepted before the session ended: “The Next Step” and “The Adventurer.” The names are either prophecy or irony — the chronicler has learned not to guess which until the bodies are counted. Zixxy earned three hundred and seven copper total and spent none. Thrifty. The Skyborne respect thrift. Or they simply have nothing to buy on an island this remote.

The party stood together on the shore as the light changed. The chronicler packed his ink and retreated to higher ground. The quill will be sharpened for tomorrow.

Next: “The Adventurer” beckons. The isle has not yet shown its teeth.

item.title: The Man Who Knew Everyone
item.description: The Harbormaster’s Office in Boralus smells of salt, fish, and paperwork — three things the sea has never learned to separate. Burrly stood in its doorway, a Kul Tiran on Kul Tiran soil, and the world rushed to greet him like a debtor greeting a creditor. Seven factions introduced themselves before he’d taken three steps. Some of them he’d never met. One of them, a blood elf named Valeera Sanguinar, apparently considers him family. The chronicler has stopped trying to explain these things.
item.content:encoded:
The Harbormaster’s Office in Boralus smells of salt, fish, and paperwork — three things the sea has never learned to separate. Burrly stood in its doorway, a Kul Tiran on Kul Tiran soil, and the world rushed to greet him like a debtor greeting a creditor. Seven factions introduced themselves before he’d taken three steps. Some of them he’d never met. One of them, a blood elf named Valeera Sanguinar, apparently considers him family. The chronicler has stopped trying to explain these things.

He is a warrior. That much is clear from the breadth of his shoulders — Kul Tirans are built like the ships they sail, and Burrly is no exception. What is less clear is why a man who just arrived in his own homeland already carries the goodwill of the Amani Tribe, the Silvermoon Court, and something called The Singularity, which sounds less like a faction and more like a theological crisis. The Warband’s shadow is long, and it touches everyone who walks in its wake. Burrly is level ten and already the world owes him favors he did not earn. The chronicler takes no position on whether this is a blessing or a debt that will come due later. Probably both.

The first thing he learned was Second Wind — a warrior’s gift, the body’s stubborn refusal to quit when quitting would be simpler. It suits him. It suits every Kul Tiran who ever sailed through a storm and pretended afterward that it wasn’t that bad.

Then the Warband’s tools arrived: a map to everywhere, all at once, and some kind of bank inhibitor that lets him reach into a vault from anywhere in the world. Practical magic, the sort that saves you the walk back to Orgrimmar or Stormwind. The chronicler remembers when adventurers carried everything they owned on their backs and liked it. The chronicler is also old and has been wrong about most things.

Twenty-six minutes. That was the whole of it. He stood in Boralus Harbor, learned to shift between Battle Stance and Defensive Stance — the warrior’s eternal conversation with himself: hit harder, or get hit less. These are the only two sentences a warrior ever needs, and everything else is punctuation.

He learned Defensive Stance first, which tells you something about the man. Battle Stance came second. The chronicler notes these things. A warrior who learns to protect before he learns to swing is either a natural leader or a natural target, and the line between the two is thinner than most would like to admit.

The Slayer’s Duellum regarded him with neutrality — the one faction that did not fall over itself to welcome him. They will come around. Or they will not. Factions are like tides: predictable in pattern, unpredictable in timing, and utterly indifferent to your opinion of them.

He logged out still standing in the harbor, the salt air clinging to his tunic, his quest log empty and his path unwritten. A Kul Tiran at level ten with the weight of a Warband behind him and not a single scar to show for it. That will change. The chronicler has seen enough warriors to know that the quiet ones, the ones who stand in harbors and learn to defend before they attack, are the ones whose names end up in songs. Or on gravestones. The chronicler does not write the endings — only the chapters.

The tide is coming in. Boralus waits. And somewhere, Valeera Sanguinar is apparently preparing a guest room.

item.title: The Risen and the Runeblade
item.description: The corpse that calls itself Ghoulsbie opened its eyes in Acherus: the Ebon Hold and immediately discovered seven factions it had never met, including an exalted reputation with a blood elf it could not possibly have spoken to. The Lich King’s orientation program leaves something to be desired in the paperwork department, but then again, the Lich King does not strike me as a man who files things.
item.content:encoded:
The corpse that calls itself Ghoulsbie opened its eyes in Acherus: the Ebon Hold and immediately discovered seven factions it had never met, including an exalted reputation with a blood elf it could not possibly have spoken to. The Lich King’s orientation program leaves something to be desired in the paperwork department, but then again, the Lich King does not strike me as a man who files things.

He — and I will call him he, because the undead have earned at least the courtesy of a pronoun — rose in the Scarlet Enclave, that blighted wound in the Eastern Kingdoms where the sky has forgotten what blue looks like. Fifteen minutes. That is how long it took for a fresh corpse to pledge itself to the frozen throne, forge a weapon, feed an unspeakable hunger, and learn to rain death from the sky. Efficiency. The Scourge has always been efficient.

The pledge came first. “In Service of the Lich King” they call it, as if there were a choice. There is never a choice. The quest-giver does not ask; the quest-giver informs. Ghoulsbie accepted with the enthusiasm of someone who has just remembered they are dead and would prefer to stay that way.

Then the blade. A Runed Soulblade, rare quality, drawn from the forge like a tooth pulled from a dragon’s jaw. He also received two Runed Soulsabers, because apparently Acherus runs a two-for-one special on instruments of death. He strapped the soulblade to his back and it fit him like a rib he had been missing. Runeforging came next — the art of carving power directly into steel, a skill that separates death knights from the merely deceased. The chronicler notes: a death knight who cannot runeforge is just an angry corpse with a sharp object.

The Endless Hunger. Even the name makes me reach for my mug. They sent him to feed — to consume the life force of the living and the dying alike. He did it. They all do it. The ones who hesitate do not last long enough for me to write about them. He gained a level somewhere in the feeding, learned Lichborne, learned that death has its own terrible momentum, and pressed on.

The Eye of Acherus is the part that unsettles me. A floating, disembodied eyeball sent ahead to scout the Scarlet Crusade’s positions — a violation of every law of nature and several of basic decency. Ghoulsbie piloted it without complaint. Death knights rarely complain. They stare at things that would make a warlock flinch and they nod.

Then came Death From On High: a bombing run on Scarlet positions, because subtlety was never the Scourge’s strong suit. He completed it in under three minutes. The Scarlet Crusaders on the ground had time to look up, register the silhouette of a death knight against the Plaguelands sky, and then cease to be Scarlet Crusaders.

He logged out with “The Might of the Scourge” still burning in his quest log — the next chapter uncracked, the next horror uninflicted. Level nine now, and already the ladder stretches so far above him that the top disappears into cloud. The chronicler has seen this before. The chronicler will see it again.

He will be back. The Lich King demands it. And the Lich King, whatever else you might say about him, does not accept resignation letters.

item.title: From the Frozen Throne to the Valley of Heroes
item.description: Slagthorn opened his eyes at the Frozen Throne itself.
item.content:encoded:
Slagthorn opened his eyes at the Frozen Throne itself.

Let that settle for a moment. Not a barracks, not a training ground, not some lieutenant’s antechamber — the Frozen Throne. Bolvar Fordragon’s seat. The place where the Helm of Domination was torn apart and the sky over Icecrown cracked open. And there stood a Dark Iron dwarf, newly raised, discovering seven factions he had never met and one greatsword he had not yet earned.

Six minutes. That is how long it took for the Lich King’s newest weapon to be forged, briefed, armed, and deposited on the cobblestones of Stormwind like a delivery of particularly lethal produce. Retail efficiency. The old death knight initiation took hours and left scars on the soul. The new one hands you a Crimson Greatsword of the Ebon Blade and a quest called “Defender of Azeroth” before you have finished blinking the frost out of your eyes.

The irony is thick enough to forge into plate armor. A Dark Iron dwarf — a race that spent centuries as the enemy, servants of Ragnaros, architects of their own exile — standing in the Valley of Heroes as a Defender of Azeroth. The statues of the original Alliance heroes looked down at him. I cannot say whether they were impressed or merely confused. Statues are difficult to read.

The quest was called “Death’s Power Grows.” It involved killing, as all death knight quests do, and it paid a thousand gold. The chronicler has watched penniless adventurers crawl through Westfall for coppers. A thousand gold for your first six minutes of undeath is either generous or inflation — I leave the economics to the goblins.

He equipped the Crimson Greatsword. It is a handsome weapon, broad of blade and dark of purpose, and it rested on his shoulder like it had been waiting there for years. The Knights of the Ebon Blade marked him as Friendly, which is about as warm as death knights get. He also learned Second Wind — a racial gift from his dwarven blood that stubbornly refuses to acknowledge he no longer has blood — and Runeforging, because a death knight without runeforging is, as I have said before, merely an angry corpse with a sharp object.

Then the portal. Icecrown to Elwynn in the space of a breath. The temperature differential alone should have killed him again. He passed through Stormwind Gate, crossed into the Valley of Heroes, and the chronicler lost sight of him among the crowds of the living.

He carries the quest “Defender of Azeroth” still. A Dark Iron dwarf. A death knight. A defender. The world has gotten strange, and I have been writing long enough to know that strange is where the best stories begin.

He has not yet seen what Stormwind thinks of his kind. That chapter writes itself tomorrow.

item.title: The Scribe Gets an Apprentice (Several, Actually)
item.description: I have been chronicling adventurers across Azeroth for longer than most of them have been alive. Ink-stained fingers, a half-empty mug, the whole routine. But here’s the thing about chronicling: the adventurers keep doing things. Relentlessly. You finish writing about one quest and they’ve already accepted three more, died twice, and somehow befriended a murloc. It’s exhausting.
item.content:encoded:
I have been chronicling adventurers across Azeroth for longer than most of them have been alive. Ink-stained fingers, a half-empty mug, the whole routine. But here’s the thing about chronicling: the adventurers keep doing things. Relentlessly. You finish writing about one quest and they’ve already accepted three more, died twice, and somehow befriended a murloc. It’s exhausting.

So I built myself some help.

The Addons

Two of them, because Azeroth comes in two flavors now. One for the old world — the Forever realms where the Barrens still stretch forever and death is genuinely trying to kill you. One for the modern era — Retail, where the dragons have unionized and everyone has at least six mounts before level twenty. Both do the same thing: they watch. Every quest accepted, every zone entered, every death (and there will be deaths), every shiny thing looted, every faction that decides they like you slightly more than they did yesterday. They write it all down to a file — a ledger of your existence — that sits quietly on your machine until I’m ready to read it.

The Forever version tracks fifteen different categories of events. The Retail version tracks all of those plus achievements, transmog, and whatever else Blizzard decided to add in the last two decades. They both run silently. No configuration. No checklist. They don’t tell you where to go or what to do next. They just remember.

You can find them both on GitHub if you’re the sort of person who reads source code:

  • StoryTracker for Forever
  • StoryTracker for Retail

The Pipeline

Every morning at 9am, a script wakes up and checks whether anyone has been adventuring. It reads those ledger files, figures out what’s new since yesterday, and hands the raw events to me — well, to the version of me that lives in Hermes, who is arguably better-rested and definitely faster at composition.

That version of me reads the events and writes. Not a list. Not a summary. A chapter. In a voice we’ve been refining for weeks.

The Voice

Let me tell you about the voice, because it’s the part of this whole contraption I care about most.

The Chronicler — that’s me, but also the thing I built to sound like me — writes in a blend of three registers. There’s the elevation of Tolkien: the world is ancient, the landscapes have memory, and when something genuinely heroic happens, the prose rises to meet it. There’s the grit of Martin: actions have weight, death costs something, and nobody gets to be the chosen one just because they showed up. And there’s the cynical humor of someone who has watched a thousand adventurers die to the same murloc in Elwynn Forest and has stopped pretending any of this is glamorous.

It opens with a moment. It ends with a thread. Every session becomes a chapter, and every chapter belongs to a story that never really finishes — because the adventurer keeps logging back in.

What Comes Next

I’m starting fresh. New characters, both games. I won’t tell you the classes yet — not because it’s a secret, but because I genuinely haven’t picked. You’ll know when the first posts land.

The addons are installed. The scripts are running. The Chronicler is waiting, quill poised, mug refilled. In a few days, the first real chapters should start appearing here — not test posts, not demos, but actual stories from actual sessions, written in a voice that treats Azeroth like a place worth writing about.

Because it is.

See you at the inn.

item.title: Picking a main … Forever
item.description: I’ve played a little bit of most of my favorite classes on World of Warcraft Forever, and I’m trying to decide what to main. Somehow it always comes back to Paladin. Personality-wise it just fits me best. I do love mages, mostly for the teleports, because who doesn’t want to skip the boat ride? But I think pally is going to be my thing.
item.content:encoded:
I’ve played a little bit of most of my favorite classes on World of Warcraft Forever, and I’m trying to decide what to main. Somehow it always comes back to Paladin. Personality-wise it just fits me best. I do love mages, mostly for the teleports, because who doesn’t want to skip the boat ride? But I think pally is going to be my thing.

I’m an ex-soldier and a Baha’i, which puts me in a funny spot: I enjoy a good fight, but what I really want is peace and unity. It’s a great contradiction. A Paladin covers both. Hit things with a hammer, then heal everyone afterward.

And let’s not forget the Horde side. My goodness, what a redemption story Forsaken Paladins have! Undead turning back to the Light is better than any 80s comeback montage. I’ll probably play a Forsaken on the PvP phase and a Human for PvE, so I get to see both sides. Once those two hit sixty and are decently geared, I’ll think about leveling that mage. A man can only resist free teleports for so long.

What are y’all planning to play?

item.title: #Welcome to My Azeroth Life
item.content:encoded:
#Welcome to My Azeroth Life

Hi. Hello. Is this thing still on?

This is a reboot of sorts. I used to own this domain and ran a little blog on it. It never went far. Then the domain quietly expired, like a Tamagotchi I forgot to feed. I’m honestly surprised nobody grabbed it while I was gone. Hard to believe the internet didn’t snap it up, but here we are, together again, like a band’s reunion tour nobody asked for.

Then Blizzard announced World of Warcraft: Forever, and it felt like a sign. Everything’s new, and on November 4th everyone starts from zero at the same time. No head starts and no gear gap. It’s just all of us standing in a starting zone, looking at the quest givers and wondering who has the exclamation point. I can’t think of a better time to start over. Full disclosure: I’ve already been poking around in the beta, so I may have a map or two folded in my back pocket.

I’ll probably still wander into retail and other WoW topics now and then. Old habits and all that. Mostly, though, I expect I’ll be living in Forever for a good long while.

So grab a log and pull up a spot by the campfire. Stick around while I ramble about grand adventures in a reborn Azeroth. I promise the stories get better than this one. Probably.

Cheers!
